opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the reputation is earned, but it's often misunderstood. The military isn't hard to sell to because people inside it don't want new technology. In my experience, there are a lot of operators and program folks who are hungry for better tools, especially in software and AI. The difficulty comes from the system around them.

You've got a budgeting process that plans two or three years out, so if you show up with a great product today, there may literally be no money allocated for it until a future fiscal year. You've got acquisition rules built for buying aircraft carriers and tanks, things with long development cycles and very defined requirements, and that model fits awkwardly with software that iterates every few weeks. On top of that you have security accreditation, authority to operate, data classification issues, and a lot of stakeholders who can say no and very few who can say yes on their own.

So for a startup, the challenge is less about convincing a single customer that your product is good and more about navigating that whole chain: finding the user who has the problem, the program office that has the money, the contracting officer who can actually write the deal, and the security people who'll let it onto the network. That takes time and patience, and a lot of companies run out of runway before they get through it. That's the so-called valley of death.

That said, it's gotten meaningfully better. Organizations like the Defense Innovation Unit, the AFWERX and SOFWERX-type efforts, other transaction authorities, and commercial solutions openings have created faster on-ramps. Leadership has also become much more vocal that they need commercial innovation, particularly in AI, autonomy, and data. So my assessment is that it's still hard, but it's no longer impossible, and companies that take the time to understand how the customer buys, not just what the customer needs, can absolutely succeed there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the reputation is earned and explains military-specific procurement obstacles; it does not compare the military with large corporate customers or argue that both are similarly hard to enter.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say the reputation is earned, but it's also a little misunderstood. The military is hard to sell to, there's no question about that. The acquisition process was built for buying aircraft carriers and tanks, things that take a decade to develop and stay in service for forty years. When you try to push software through that same pipeline, especially something like AI that changes every six months, you get friction. The budget cycles are long, the requirements are written years in advance, and by the time something gets funded, the technology has already moved on.

But here's what people miss. The difficulty isn't really about the customer not wanting the product. The warfighters, the operators, the people actually doing the mission, they're incredibly hungry for better tools. I've sat in rooms with folks who are frustrated because they know what's possible and they can't get it. The problem is the distance between that end user and the person who actually holds the checkbook. You might have ten layers of people between those two points, and every one of them has a legitimate reason to say no. Security, compliance, interoperability, sustainment. None of those concerns are wrong, they just stack up.

So when companies say the military is impossible to sell to, what they usually mean is they showed up with a commercial playbook. They expected a sales cycle of a few months and a champion who could sign a contract. That's just not how it works. You have to be willing to invest for years, understand the mission, go through the accreditation process, and build relationships across the whole chain. The companies that succeed are the ones that treat it as a long-term commitment rather than a quick win. And honestly, the Department has gotten better. Things like the Defense Innovation Unit and other transaction authorities have opened doors that didn't exist a decade ago. It's still hard, but it's hard in ways you can plan for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the military is difficult to sell to and explains its acquisition barriers, but it does not compare that difficulty with breaking into large corporate customers or argue that the reputation is unfair on that basis.

astra-6.text:
I think that reputation is deserved in some ways, but it needs context. The military is a huge organization, and the person who needs your product isn’t necessarily the person who controls the budget or the person who can buy it. You can have an enthusiastic customer and still have a long road to a contract.

The key is understanding a specific problem and who’s responsible for solving it. If you show up saying, “We have great AI; what can you do with it?” you’re making the customer do the work. If you can explain how you’ll help them accomplish a mission, and demonstrate that reliably, you have a much better starting point. But you still have to understand the buying process. Operational interest and an actual purchase are two separate hurdles.

r001.rationale: The response gives context for why selling to the military is difficult, but it does not argue that the reputation is unfair by comparing the military with large corporate customers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that reputation is earned. The military can be a very difficult customer, particularly for a small company. You can have a user who loves your product and a real problem you can solve, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that person has the budget or the authority to buy it. Those are separate things, and navigating that process takes time.

But I think it’s important to distinguish between selling to the military and working with the people who actually use the technology. If you can get in front of those people, understand their problem, and demonstrate something that makes their job easier, you can build a lot of enthusiasm. The challenge is turning that enthusiasm into a purchase. So I wouldn’t say, “Don’t sell to the military.” I’d say, “Understand the buying process, and make sure your company can survive how long it takes.”

r001.rationale: The candidate says the military’s difficult-customer reputation is earned and discusses its buying process, but does not compare it with large corporate customers or argue the reputation is unfair.
